problem: ANN-based embodied navigation agents rely on dense computation and degrade sharply under visual corruptions (blur, noise, etc.). SNN advantages have mostly been shown on frame-level perception or simple mapless/lidar navigation, not visually rich indoor navigation.
motivation: Compact, disturbance-tolerant navigation is needed for resource-constrained cyber-physical platforms. Spiking neurons' membrane integration, thresholding and reset may suppress transient visual perturbations in closed-loop decision making, but it is unclear whether this holds in visually grounded PointNav/ObjectNav.
key_idea: Replace both the perception encoder and the recurrent policy core of a standard actor-critic navigation agent with spiking modules (SSE + SPN, using native integrate-and-fire membrane state as the recurrent policy state), improving robustness to visual corruptions at lower cost.
insight: The robustness gain comes from spiking perception coupled with spiking policy dynamics, not from a more robust static feature extractor. On ImageNet-C the SNN encoder is actually less robust than the ResNet (31.32% vs 34.41%), yet the full agent retains 40.18% of clean ObjectNav SR vs 27.21% for ANNNav. The ablation shows SSE-only (9.58 SR) and SPN-only (10.20) both help modestly, while the full model (13.71) is best, indicating complementary roles. A proposition states that if perturbation stays below the spike margin, the spike pattern is preserved.
method: Spiking Sensing Encoder (SSE): a spike-based ResNet18-style backbone (T=4 internal steps, from BURST) plus a 2-conv compressor gives a 7x7x32 visual feature; the goal (object-category embedding or PointNav goal descriptor) is spatially tiled and concatenated, then fused by two conv layers and flattened.

Spiking Policy Network (SPN): a recurrent core with v_t = λu_{t-1} + W_r r_t + W_h u_{t-1}, spike s_t = H(v_t − ϑ), and reset u_t = v_t ⊙ (1 − s_t). The post-reset membrane state is the policy state h_t, with linear softmax actor and linear critic heads. Native IF dynamics are used rather than a Spiking-GRU.
Training: PPO actor-critic in AllenAct with surrogate gradients for the spike function (value coef 0.5, entropy coef 0.01), no changes to the RL task interface.

Temporal robustness analysis: a perturbation budget B_{τ,j} is compared with the minimum spike margin. If B < margin, the spike pattern is preserved and the actor-logit change is bounded by ||W_π|| B.
ANNNav matched baseline: a re-implementation of the RobustNav DD-PPO pipeline with identical data, training and evaluation, used for the ablation and for the params/FLOPs comparison.
Neuromorphic deployment: the SSE is mapped onto one core of the taped-out Thruster-V2 chip (5 V, 625 MHz) and cycles, current and energy are measured.

setting.backbone: Spiking ResNet18-style encoder + spiking recurrent policy (SPN), trained from scratch with PPO
setting.training_data: RoboTHOR PointNav / ObjectNav episodes via online RL in AllenAct; no extra data
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (RGB-D configurable) + goal (object category token or point-goal vector)
setting.action_space: discrete low-level actions (standard AllenAct RoboTHOR action set)
setting.simulator: RoboTHOR (AI2-THOR), with RobustNav visual corruptions; SSE deployed on Thruster-V2 chip

numbers.extra: clean observations; trained in the same AllenAct pipeline as ANNNav
numbers.evidence: Table 2 (Model scale and clean performance): SpikingNav 12.1M, 0.97G, ObjectNav 34.12 / 16.20; Table 1 rounds to 34.1/16.2

numbers.extra: average over seven corruptions (low lighting, motion blur, camera crack, defocus blur, speckle noise, lower FOV, spatter)

numbers_note: The benchmark is RoboTHOR (not in the canonical list), and the split is not stated explicitly. Per-corruption results are given only in Fig. 2, not in tables. The neuromorphic chip results are not navigation metrics.
results: SpikingNav improves clean ObjectNav SR from 31.05 to 34.12 and corrupted-average SR from 8.45 to 13.71 over the matched ANNNav, with fewer params (12.1M vs 14.0M) and much lower FLOPs (0.97G vs 4.21G). On PointNav it is slightly below ANNNav on clean data (96.54 vs 98.21 SR, 72.93 vs 82.13 SPL) but more robust under several corruptions. It remains far below CLIP/LLM-based ObjectNav systems (EmbCLIP 47.0, SG-Nav 47.5 SR).
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation, and hardware validation covers only the SSE (2.133G cycles, 3.92 J per sample), not the closed-loop agent, so energy efficiency is not shown to be better.
Only compact models are studied, and it is unclear whether the benefits hold for large VLA models. Clean PointNav SPL is lower than ANNNav's, and ObjectNav SR is far below large-model methods.
Robustness evidence is empirical, on one simulator and a single ANN baseline, and the proposition is a sufficient condition with no verification that it holds in practice.
